title: AI in Education #7: Five Things I Learned from Bibi Groot About What Happens When You Actually Test Whether AI Tutoring Works
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton talks with Bibi Groot, Eedi's first behavioural scientist, about two years of randomised controlled trials testing whether Eedi's platform and AI tutoring actually help students learn. A 20-school, 3,448-student RCT independently evaluated by Professor Steve Higgins found no measurable effect at six months but an effect size of 0.17 at twelve months, rising to 0.46 at eighteen months, which Groot says shows why short ed-tech studies and the file-drawer problem distort what the field thinks works. A separate Google DeepMind trial then pitted a constrained AI tutor against expert human tutors and static hints with 165 students: on same-question retries the human and AI tutors both topped 90 percent versus 65 percent for static hints, but on transfer to a related question the AI tutor (66 percent) beat the human tutor (60 percent), which Groot attributes to the AI consistently using Socratic questioning that experienced human tutors tended to skip. Two further studies caution against unconstrained chatbot use: a Turkish RCT found students who practised with GPT-4 performed worse on a subsequent closed-book exam than students with no AI access, and a companion study found the same pattern with on-demand chess hints. Groot describes Eedi's AI tutor as deliberately constrained - activating only after a wrong answer, unable to receive screenshots, and stripped of student demographic data after a Stanford study found an AI feedback tool gave differential praise by race. A follow-up Google DeepMind trial now running in 10 UK schools with 1,200 students will test whether knowing pedagogy or knowing the individual student matters more, with results due by September 2026.
points: The Eedi RCT (20 schools, 3,448 students, independently run by Professor Steve Higgins' team) found zero measurable effect at six months but an effect size of 0.17 at twelve months and 0.46 at eighteen months, showing that short ed-tech trials risk wrongly concluding an intervention doesn't work.

In the Google DeepMind RCT, a constrained AI tutor beat both an expert human tutor and static hints on transfer to a new but related question (66% vs 60% vs 56%), which Groot attributes to the AI's consistent Socratic questioning versus human tutors' tendency to fix the misconception quickly.

A Turkish high-school RCT found students who practised maths with unrestricted GPT-4 access performed worse on a later closed-book exam than students given no AI access at all, evidence that unconstrained chatbot use can actively harm learning rather than just fail to help it.

Eedi's AI tutor is deliberately constrained in five specific ways (only activates after a wrong answer, no screenshots, guided questioning, ends on resolution) and is withheld all student demographic data, after a Stanford study found an AI feedback tool gave Black students softer feedback than white students.

The next Google DeepMind trial (10 UK schools, 1,200 students, due September 2026) isolates whether an AI tutor with strong pedagogy knowledge or one with deep knowledge of the individual student produces better outcomes.
quotes: For years, I just assumed Eedi was effective. I had built it. I believed in the pedagogy behind it.
Bibi made the point that a lot of ed-tech companies run short studies, find positive results, and announce them. But the file drawer problem is real
One tutor said afterwards: "The AI is giving the kind of feedback I would like to give if I had more time.

The students who had practised with AI did worse. They had offloaded the cognitive work to the chatbot, and when it was taken away, they had less in their heads than the students who had struggled on their own.

Michael Pershan says that any tutor that the tutee can control is not a tutor. Adam Boxer went further in our conversation, saying schools should be communicating to students that using AI is a waste of their time.
About 75% of the AI's suggested messages were approved and sent without any edits. Of the 25% that were edited, roughly half were small tweaks
She thinks static content will come last. She thinks the human tutor and the pedagogy-only AI will be roughly on par. And she hopes the context-rich AI will come out on top
when an AI writing feedback tool was given access to student demographic data - gender and ethnicity - it gave Black students more praise and softer feedback than white students.
